rewrites.summary:
For a same-sex couple travelling together, the core legal situation is recognition without status: a 2020 Court of Appeal ruling requires overseas marriages to be recognised, and immigration authorities did recognise such a marriage — the same-sex marriage ban struck down in March 2019 was overturned on appeal in August 2019, but the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. Since 2022, however, a statute confines family status to heterosexual marriage, and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it, so same-sex partners hold no local marriage or civil-partnership status and the parent country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue.

Enforcement context: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. Practical safety is comparatively benign: roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the first Pride parade in July 2021, one of the broadest official turnouts the community has seen, although organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection amid public-space sensitivities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-authority policy turbulence frames the later recognition rulings: in 2009 UK legislators on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires, while the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended.
rewrites.localsOnly: For residents, family law is the contested terrain: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect in 2022, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself. The March 2019 strike-down of the same-sex marriage ban by the Grand Court was overturned on appeal in August 2019; only the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of the United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary. No source documents border-screening practice, arrest patterns, or the operational fate of the unequal age of consent, so those parts of the visitor picture rest on the recognition rulings and the 2001 decriminalisation alone.

rewrites.summary:
For a same-sex couple travelling together, same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the administering country's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act. Family status remains contested: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the United Kingdom, who sought recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success, leaving the recognition judgment standing.

Practical safety: travel surveys rate this destination among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, and most visitors hardly notice either way — discretion, not danger, is the operative norm for a visitor.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-authority policy pivots set the baseline: in January 2001 the administering country scrapped the homosexuality laws across the Caribbean region by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act, and a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed.
rewrites.localsOnly: For residents, family status is litigated rather than settled: court cases test whether same-sex marriages are valid under local law, and the 2022 refusal of the churches council's appeal bid left the recognition judgment standing. The travel-profile source describes most local hostility as 'silent and invisible', with secret lives beneath the tolerant surface — a resident social-climate reading.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of the United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary. The gay-welcoming characterisation rests on an undated travel profile (2012/2017), so it cannot be verified against current conditions, and no source documents border-screening practice or arrest patterns for visitors.

rewrites.summary:
The controlling finding for a transgender visitor is judicial, from early October 2023: the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that the 'femicide' offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in the penal code — covers only 'a person biologically female'. On that operative interpretation, applied where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction over Tarapacá, the most severe legal protection available for gender-motivated violence does not extend to trans women in this region.

Practical context: Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the nationally documented anti-LGBTI case total in 2024 and ranked among the fastest-rising regions (+18.18 % year-on-year), a small-share region in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal; absolute case volume is small.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Regional-comparison context colours the finding rather than adding local risk: versus national 0.72 the region sits at −0.08; versus the compared region La Araucanía (0.65) it is 0.01 lower because that region's −0.07 is trend-based (+150 % rise, low visibility) rather than ruling-based; and versus the other compared region Arica y Parinacota (0.69) it is 0.05 lower because the Iquique annulment is a documented finding within Tarapacá's own judicial district, whereas the other region's deviation rests on the shared northern-court context with no trans-specific incident of its own.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing case facts: the victim was a 55-year-old trans woman whose body was found on the southern coast of the provincial capital in June 2022; her killer was convicted at first instance to presidio perpetuo, and on the defence's nullity motion the Iquique court declared the sentence void in early October 2023. The national legal framework (Law 21.120 and the femicide article) remains on the books.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The case-share figures (1.56 % of the national total; +18.18 % year-on-year) rest on the annual-report dataset, which no region-specific source independently covers. No source documents border-screening practice, documents handling, or marriage/partner-travel matters for transgender visitors in this region, so the visitor assessment rests on the judicial finding and the case-share signal alone.
